subject: Post-call: E2E tail latency routing & scaling playbook
messages:
From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.ai>
To: Ava Green <ava@acme.ai>; Ethan Cho <ethan.cho@acme.ai>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-09-28T22:12:00Z
Subject: Post-call recap — E2E tail latency targets and routing questions

Thanks for the time today — short recap and proposed next steps from our side. High-level takeaways from the call:

- Acme target: p95 end-to-end ~= 150ms, p99 end-to-end <= 400ms for the customer-facing routing.
- Workload notes: many short streaming responses (avg 120 tokens), heavy burstiness during campaign windows (~6x baseline for 10–15 minutes).
- Current provider: you reported larger tail behavior on p99 for streaming (more on that below).

Open questions / items we need from you to finalize a playbook:
1) Full request traces (ingress headers + timing) from a 1-hour spike window — prefer HAR or similar.
2) Typical concurrency distribution (95/99 concurrency), and a short list of routes prioritized for low tail latency.
3) Any SIM/edge policies (CDN or DNS warmup) that affect cold-starts.

Our immediate proposal (to validate hosted route fit):
- Canary routing plan: run a 48h controlled canary with 2 traffic splits (5% then 25%) across two routing strategies:
  * Direct-hosted: route -> Redwood hosted model (quantized variant) with per-route caching + streaming enabled.
  * Fallback path: routing -> incumbent provider for sustained bursts based on pre-defined thresholds.
- SLO probes: continuous p50/p95/p99 SLO evaluation at 1-min granularity, synthetic traces that mirror your spike pattern.
- Concurrency shaping: allow for adaptive batching up to X tokens and a concurrency cap at 400 sessions (tunable).

Attachments: I’m attaching a quick snapshot of the p95 profile we saw in the demo and a draft routing playbook (routing-playbook-draft.md) — should help clarify implementation steps.

Next steps: if you can send the traces and the prioritized route list by EOD 2026-09-29, we’ll finalize the canary config and schedule the first 5% traffic run for 2026-10-04.

Best,
Markus Klein
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
[attachment: routing-playbook-draft.md (text)]

From: Ava Green <ava@acme.ai>
To: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.ai>
Cc: ops@acme.ai; Ethan Cho <ethan.cho@acme.ai>
Date: 2026-09-29T08:14:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call recap — E2E tail latency targets and routing questions

Thanks Markus — good summary. Quick answers and what we attached:

- We attached: request_trace_20260928.har (1-hour spike capture) and a short CSV with per-route QPS and concurrent sessions.
- Current provider numbers (observed during the spike): p95 ~= 260ms e2e; p99 spikes to 1.2s (streaming sessions show chunking-gap behavior).
- Concurrency: typical baseline ~80 concurrent sessions, during campaign peaks we see ~480 concurrent sessions (sustained for ~12 minutes).
- Streaming details: client uses 8KB chunks with a client-side keepalive at 5s; partial chunk latency contributes heavily to p99.

Two clarifying asks for Redwood:
1) How does your prefix/KV cache treat streaming sessions vs non-streaming? We need the streaming partial-chunk latencies to be accounted for in SLOs.
2) If we route 5% traffic initially, how do you ensure DNS-based warmup and regional affinity for low tail outcomes?

We uploaded the HAR and the CSV to the drive link you shared.

— Ava
Ava Green
Head of Platform Engineering, Acme AI
[attachment: request_trace_20260928.har (har)]

Markus — tagging for alignment. Quick notes from the commercial side:

- If the canary proves we can hit p95=150ms / p99<=400ms at 25% traffic, we should be prepared to offer a 60-day credit guardrail for initial rollout. Finance is ok with a one-time credit if we miss SLO in the first 30 days (TBD).

Ben

From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.ai>
To: Ava Green <ava@acme.ai>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai, lauren_bishop@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-09-30T16:46:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call recap — E2E tail latency targets and routing questions

Appreciate the quick turnaround and trace uploads, Ava. I reviewed the HAR and CSV; highlights and updated playbook items below.

Highlights from our trace review:
- The HAR confirms chunking gaps around client keepalive boundaries — we can smooth this with a small client-side tweak (reduce keepalive to 2s) or by enabling our streaming jitter buffer on the hosted path.
- Baseline path (non-spike) looks capable of hitting p95 ~120–160ms for prioritized routes with our quantized variants and per-route prefix caching.
- During spikes, the majority of p99 blowups correlate with queueing during concurrency bursts and a few long tail kernel-level stalls on the incumbent provider traces.

Updated playbook (attached):
- Pre-canary: DNS pre-seed 1 hour, provision reserved capacity for expected 6x peak (autoscale headroom disabled for first 5% window).
- Canary windows: 5% (24h) -> evaluate SLOs -> 25% (48h) if stable -> 100% progressive rollout.
- Probes: synthetic replay of the HAR at 1.5x to validate headroom; collect p50/p95/p99 and streaming chunk latency.
- Fallback threshold: if p99 exceeds 400ms for >5 consecutive 1-min intervals or error rate >0.5%, switch fallback routing for affected route.

Next steps:
- Marissa: confirm reserved capacity numbers and attach estimated incremental cost to this thread.
- Ben: finalize the credit guardrail language and confirm with finance.
- Ava/Ethan: confirm if you prefer client keepalive change or want us to enable streaming jitter buffer on the hosted path.

I’ve attached the current routing-playbook-draft.md with the DNS steps and probe definitions. If everyone is aligned I’ll lock the canary config and request the 5% start date for 2026-10-04.

Thanks — Markus
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
